activities.anchor: Watch the pipeline work on one line of a made-up language
activities.caption: one sentence through the funnel, in order
activities.name: compFunnelOrder

config.prompt: One sentence — total = price + 4 * 2 — through the funnel. Put the stages' actions in order:
items: The lexer groups characters into seven tokens, whitespace discarded
The parser builds the AST — an assignment node, an addition node, a multiplication node
The grammar gives * higher precedence than +, so the tree is price + (4 * 2)
The semantic analyser walks the tree with the symbol table — was price ever declared?
The optimiser folds 4 * 2 to 8 — a provably-equivalent rewrite
config.why: Each stage checks something before passing the work down — verification rides the translation all the way to silicon.

activities.anchor: A program can be perfectly grammatical and still meaningless
activities.caption: file each complaint by the stage that raises it
activities.name: compErrorSort

config.prompt: File each complaint by the stage that raises it:

items.label: an identifier starting with a digit
'price was never declared' — absent from the symbol table
a string added to a number
the tokens arrive in an order the grammar forbids
'colourless green ideas sleep furiously' — well-formed English that means nothing

config.why: Each check is cheapest at its own level — spelling, then grammar, then sense.

activities.anchor: each stage is a small program whose only job is to load the next
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the chain from nothing to running
activities.name: compBootCloze

config.text: Power on, and the CPU executes %%0%% stored on the motherboard: it runs the power-on self-test, finds the boot device, loads the %%1%% from the disk's boot sector, and the bootloader loads the OS %%2%% into RAM and hands over.
config.hint: Small programs loading bigger ones — nothing useful was in RAM when the chain began.

activities.anchor: yet a keyboard is pressed perhaps ten times a minute
activities.caption: call the polling bill
activities.name: compPollEst

config.prompt: A 3 GHz CPU polling one device 100 times a second — roughly how many idle cycles per second does that burn?
config.why: Hundreds of millions of idle cycles — all for a device used about ten moments per minute; the interrupt replaces the question with a signal.
config.context: Attention spent only when there is news: the device raises it, the CPU looks up the routine's address and runs it.

activities.caption: pair each translator with its behaviour
activities.name: compTranslatorMatch

config.prompt: Pair each tool with its behaviour:

pairs.right: converts assembly to machine code essentially one-for-one — fast, unforgiving
translates a whole program before it runs — full-speed execution, no translator present
reads and executes a statement at a time, stopping at the first error
watches which code runs hot and compiles just those parts, with assumptions from actual runtime behaviour

config.why: There is no clean line between compiled and interpreted — only points along a spectrum of how much is translated in advance.

activities.anchor: The explosion of languages is not indecision
activities.caption: walk the language-design fork
activities.name: compTradeBranch

config.root: You are designing a language. Walk the fork in the road.

choices.label: Before running — static typing
choices.feedback: C, Rust, TypeScript: earlier error catching, more optimisation fuel — and more ceremony at write time.

choices.label: At run time — dynamic typing
choices.feedback: Python, JavaScript: faster to write, errors surface later — the runtime pays for the flexibility.

dynamic.text: Dynamic chosen. Now memory. Who frees it?

choices.label: A garbage collector
choices.feedback: Java, Go — safe, with occasional pauses; the runtime does the bookkeeping.

choices.label: The programmer, manually
choices.feedback: C — fast and dangerous; one forgotten free is a bug class.

choices.label: The compiler, via ownership rules
choices.feedback: Rust — safe and fast, harder to learn: the borrow checker is the price.

choices.label: Ownership rules — the borrow checker
choices.feedback: Rust's point in the space: safe and fast, harder to learn.

gc.text: Garbage collection trades pauses for safety; ownership trades a learning curve for both — every point on the dial is a choice, not progress.

manual.text: Manual management buys speed and sells danger — device drivers and bootloaders still pay it deliberately.

owner.text: Ownership: the borrow checker proves safety at compile time — safe and fast, harder to learn.

config.why: Typing, memory management, paradigms — choices, not progress toward one perfect language.

activities.anchor: in what was once the slowest language class in common use
activities.caption: true or false — the JIT reversal
activities.name: compJitJudge

statements.s: Compiled programs are always faster than interpreted ones.
statements.why: Modern JIT systems watch which code runs hot, compile just those parts with assumptions from actual runtime behaviour, and outperform naive ahead-of-time compilation.

statements.s: JavaScript engines render modern 3D games at 60 frames a second.
statements.why: A full reversal for a category long considered hopeless.

statements.s: JIT compilation already uses machine learning to predict hot code before it runs.
statements.why: That is an open question — prediction before the fact remains research; today's JITs measure and react.

statements.s: There is a clean line between compiled and interpreted languages.
statements.why: Java and Python both compile to bytecode for a virtual machine — only points along a spectrum of how much is translated in advance.

activities.caption: which curve is the finite automaton?
activities.name: compBracketTrace

config.prompt: Memory use against input length while counting nested brackets — which curve is the finite automaton's attempt?

curves.label: curve A — no memory at all
curve B — grows with depth (a stack)

config.why: The finite automaton has no memory beyond its current state — nested structures cannot be lexed, only parsed; the stack of a context-free grammar is what the count requires.
